newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China's legislature for HK called rubber stamp.
newsitem.headline: China's legislature for HK called rubber stamp.

text.p: The leader of Hong Kong's Democratic Party said on Sunday candidates for the legislature that China plans to establish when it regains control of the territory next year would be doing Beijing's "dirty work".

"I wonder how many of these candidates know what Beijing expects them to do -- namely to rubber stamp laws on subversion, reinstate repressive colonial laws and to repeal the most important parts of the Bill of Rights Ordinance," party chairman Martin Lee said.
"Yes, Beijing wants them to do the dirty work," he said in a radio commentary.
A three-week registration period for candidates seeking seats on the provisional legislature opened last Monday and more than 140 applications have already been collected.
The interim body is being set up by China to replace the British colony's current fully-elected council after Beijing was upset by electoral reforms enacted over its vehement objections.

Its 60 members will be chosen on December 21 by a 400-strong Selection Committee formed under China's close supervision. The same body is also choosing Hong Kong's first post-colonial chief executive. The public has no vote in either process.
Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30, 1997, and the new council is to be officially seated after that. But it is expected to meet earlier to discuss legislation.
Lee's Democratic Party, the largest in the current council, has denounced the provisional legislature as illegal and has refused to take part in it.

"So, as of Christmas this year, we're going to have one territory, two legislatures -- one defending our system and the other defending China's system," said Lee, referring to Beijing's promise of allowing capitalist Hong Kong a large measure of autonomy under a one-country, two-systems policy.
Despite Lee's warnings, the democratic camp has been divided over the new provisional legislature.
Last Wednesday, a member of the Democratic Party broke ranks and said he would apply to join the new council.
"The provisional legislature will be set up. It is inevitable," Chan Choi-hi said.

Earlier in the week, another pro-democracy party, the Association for Democracy and People's Livelihood, suffered a split when 16 of its members quit because of a decision by the leadership to seek seats in the new body.
